content: The correct use of contraceptive methods, potential complications during use (such as vomiting, diarrhea, menstrual irregularities, pelvic inflammatory disease, or pregnancy), and programmatic issues are critical considerations in family planning. This document is intended for national-level policymakers and family planning program managers. It is not designed to serve as a direct guideline for national family planning and reproductive health programs but rather as a reference for developing guidelines for contraceptive service delivery. The guidance provided in this document is meant to be interpreted at the country and program levels, taking into account the diverse contexts and settings in which contraceptives are provided. Policymakers and program managers can use this guidance to develop national standards and protocols. While the recommendations themselves are unlikely to change during this process, their application at the country level may vary significantly, depending on factors such as the clinical expertise of providers and the resources available at service delivery points. The development of these guidelines involved a Guideline Development Group (GDG) convened by the World Health Organization (WHO), comprising 68 individuals representing a broad range of stakeholders. Their mandate was to review and revise the guidance from the second edition of the Selected Practice Recommendations for Contraceptive Use (SPR) (2004) and the 2008 SPR update. GDG meetings were held in May 2013, March 2014, and September 2014. During this revision process, the GDG prioritized the review of 19 topics, including the inclusion of five new contraceptive methods: a two-rod levonorgestrel implant (Sino-implant II®), subcutaneously administered DMPA, the contraceptive patch, the contraceptive vaginal ring (CVR), and ulipristal acetate emergency contraceptive pills (UPA-ECPs). Additionally, they addressed the question of when a woman can resume or start regular contraception after using emergency contraception. The recommendations in this document are based on the latest clinical and epidemiological data, summarized in 14 systematic reviews. When direct evidence was unavailable, indirect evidence was considered, such as extrapolation from similar contraceptive methods or proxy measures of clinical outcomes. For example, evidence on combined oral contraceptives (COCs) was used to inform recommendations for the patch and CVR, and markers of ovulation were used as a proxy for pregnancy risk. An additional systematic review on values and preferences of contraceptive users was conducted to inform the development of these recommendations. The GDG considered GRADE evidence profiles, indirect evidence, the benefits of preventing unintended pregnancies, and patient values and preferences. The aim was to prioritize the availability of a wide range of contraceptive options and remove unnecessary medical barriers, thereby improving access to contraceptive services. In this updated edition of the SPR, the GDG classified recommendations as either strong or conditional. A strong recommendation is one that can be adopted as policy in most situations, while a conditional recommendation requires substantial debate and stakeholder involvement before becoming policy. Most recommendations in this edition are presented in narrative form, but for recommendations related to examinations and tests for the safe provision of contraceptive methods, an A-B-C classification scale is applied. This scale, developed by the expert group for the first edition of the SPR in 2001, has been retained to avoid confusion among guideline users. The WHO will review all recommendations in this document in four years. In the interim, WHO will continue to monitor the evidence base and convene additional consultations if new evidence necessitates reconsideration of existing recommendations. Updates may be particularly warranted for issues where the evidence base evolves rapidly. WHO also encourages research to address unresolved issues related to the safe and effective use of contraceptives and invites comments and suggestions for improving this guidance. The SPR provides guidance on the safe and effective use of contraceptive methods, aiming to improve access to and quality of family planning services. It is intended to assist policymakers, decision-makers, and program managers in developing or revising national guidelines for the provision of hormonal contraceptives, intrauterine devices, barrier methods, fertility awareness-based methods, sterilization, and emergency contraception. The document emphasizes a rights-based approach to reproductive and sexual health care, recognizing it as a human right and a key intervention for improving health outcomes. Reproductive rights encompass the basic right of all individuals to decide freely and responsibly the number, spacing, and timing of their children, and to have the information and means to do so. These rights also include the highest attainable standard of sexual and reproductive health. International agreements, such as the 1994 International Conference on Population and Development (ICPD) and the 1995 Beijing Declaration, underscore the importance of reproductive rights as part of human rights. Access to contraceptive information and services is recognized as a human right, and states are obligated to ensure timely and affordable access to high-quality sexual and reproductive health services. These services should respect individual privacy, dignity, autonomy, and informed decision-making, and be sensitive to the needs and perspectives of clients. A rights-based approach to contraceptive provision considers clients' sexual and reproductive health needs and ensures that eligibility criteria do not create unnecessary barriers to access. Evidence shows that respecting, protecting, and fulfilling human rights contributes to positive health outcomes. Providing contraceptive information and services that respect privacy, confidentiality, and informed choice, along with a wide range of safe contraceptive methods, increases satisfaction and continued use of contraception. Delivering care in accordance with clients' human and reproductive rights is fundamental to quality care. The development of international norms for medical eligibility criteria and practice recommendations for contraceptive use is one aspect of improving reproductive health care quality. Family planning programs should include screening, treatment, and follow-up procedures that reflect high standards of public health and clinical practice, but these should not be seen as eligibility requirements for specific contraceptive methods. Examples include screening and treatment for cervical cancer, anemia, and sexually transmitted infections (STIs), as well as promoting breastfeeding and smoking cessation. While this document primarily addresses specific contraceptive practices, social, behavioral, and non-medical criteria, particularly client preferences, must also be considered. Providing contraceptive choices in a way that respects and fulfills clients' human rights requires enabling them to make informed decisions.
